# Polynesian and Micronesian wayfinding (`polynesian_wayfinding`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by world_geography, wind_systems_ocean_currents
- Core idea: Without instruments, navigators steer by the rising and setting points of memorised stars on the horizon (a 'star compass' of about 32 houses), by the direction of the long ocean swells felt through the hull, by sun and wind, and they expand a small island into a wide target using signs: land birds such as terns and noddies fly out up to 30–50 km at dawn and return at dusk, clouds pile up and turn greenish over lagoons, swells bend around islands. Double-hulled canoes 15–20 m long with crab-claw sails carried families, plants and animals over thousands of kilometres, often sailing upwind first so that home lay downwind.
- Pitfalls:
  - Calling the settlement of the Pacific accidental drift; computer simulations and the 1976 Hokule'a voyage Hawaii–Tahiti without instruments refute that
  - Dating it too early or too late; East Polynesia was settled quickly c. 1000–1300 AD after a long pause
  - Assuming the methods transfer to a European ship with a crew that has not learned them from childhood
- History: global: Pacific – c. 1200–900 BC Lapita voyagers reach Fiji, Tonga, Samoa; c. 1000–1300 AD Hawaii, Rapa Nui, New Zealand; pre-European contact with Indigenous Americans supported by genetic evidence; Marshall Islands stick charts of swell patterns; 1769 Tupaia draws a chart of some 70 islands for Cook; 1976 Hokule'a (Mau Piailug)
- Read:
  - David Lewis, We, the Navigators: The Ancient Art of Landfinding in the Pacific (1972)
  - Ben Finney, Voyage of Rediscovery: A Cultural Odyssey through Polynesia (1994)
  - J. Víctor Moreno-Mayar et al., Ancient Rapanui genomes reveal resilience and pre-European contact with the Americas, Nature 633 (2024)
  - Janet M. Wilmshurst et al., High-precision radiocarbon dating shows recent and rapid initial human colonization of East Polynesia, PNAS 108 (2011)
